subject: Copywriting
title: The Power of Specificity
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Power of Specificity usable.

hook.text: 'We helped thousands' is weak. 'We helped 2,437 businesses grow 34% in 90 days' is strong. Specificity is proof.

buildup.text: Specific numbers feel researched. Round numbers feel guessed.

discovery.text: Specific details create a halo of credibility.

twist.text: Fabricating specific numbers is fraud and will be caught. The specificity must be real. Honesty enables the technique.

climax.text: Replace every vague word in your sales letter with a number, a date, or a name.

quiz.question: Why does $97 feel more credible than $100?
options: Specific numbers feel calculated, not guessed

details.summary: In sales letters, specific claims crush vague ones. 'We've helped 14,847 customers save an average of $237.43 per month' is infinitely more persuasive than 'we've helped thousands save money.' Specificity signals measurement, which signals truthfulness.
details.whyItMatters: Specificity is the simplest upgrade any copywriter can make to increase credibility. Replacing every vague claim with a precise one transforms amateur copy into professional-grade persuasion.
takeaways: Precise numbers are perceived as measured facts, not marketing estimates
Odd, non-round numbers feel more authentic than round ones
Specificity applies to results, timelines, features, and guarantees

faq.question: Why do specific numbers feel more trustworthy?
faq.answer: The brain interprets precision as evidence of careful measurement. '$9,847' implies someone actually calculated the figure. '$10,000' feels like a round estimate — possibly inflated. This cognitive shortcut makes precise claims more believable even when both are equally accurate.

faq.question: Can you be too specific in a sales letter?
faq.answer: Only if the specificity is irrelevant or overwhelming. Be specific about things that matter to the buyer — results, savings, timelines, and guarantees. Don't overload with technical specifications that add detail without adding persuasive value.
